Description: explicit — omitted glyphs field, text renders in wrong font
prompt: My MapLibre GL JS stylesheet has no `glyphs` property set at all, and my symbol layers have `text-font` set to a font name. Text labels are showing up, but in a generic font, not the one I specified. Is this a bug I need to fix, or expected behavior? What's actually happening?
[groq-gpt-oss] evals/prompts/lib/skill-p:
### Short answer **It’s not a bug.** When a style **doesn’t contain a `glyphs` URL**, MapLibre GL JS (≥ 5.11.0) falls back to **“local-fonts mode”**. Your `text-font` values are treated exactly like a CSS `font-family` list: the library asks the browser (or the `font-faces` mapping you provide) to load the named font and draws the text with whatever font it can find. If the requested font isn’t available locally, the browser picks a generic fallback (usually *sans-serif*), which is why you see a “generic” look. Below is a deeper dive into **what’s happening**, **why it’s expected**, and **what you can do** to get the exact font you want. --- ## 1. What MapLibre GL JS does when `glyphs` is missing | Step | What the engine does | Result | |------|----------------------|--------| | **1️⃣ Style parsing** | No `glyphs` field → “local-fonts mode” is activated. | The engine knows it must not request glyph PBFs. | | **2️⃣ Resolve `text-font`** | The `text-font` array is interpreted as a **fallback list of font-family names** (just like CSS). | Example: `["MyCustom Bold", "Noto Sans Regular"]`. | | **3️⃣ Load the font** | - If the name matches a **`font-faces` entry** → the URL(s) in that entry are fetched (browser-side).
- Otherwise the browser looks for a **system-installed font** or a **web-font you have added via `@font-face` CSS**. | If a matching font is found → it is used.
If not → the browser falls back to its generic family (usually `sans-serif`). | | **4️⃣ Render** | Text is rasterised on-the-fly with **TinySDF** (an SDF generator that works on any font). | The visual result is a clean, scalable label, but the *shape* depends on the actual font that was loaded. | > **Key point:** No glyph-PBFs are ever requested, and the engine never fails the tile because of missing glyphs. The fallback is *by design* and works on all browsers that support the Font Loading API. --- ## 2. Why you see a “generic” font 1. **The font name you wrote in `text-font` does not match any locally-available font.** *E.g.* `"MyBrandFont Bold"` while the actual font file is named `"MyBrandFont-Bold.ttf"` or the CSS `font-family` is `"MyBrand Font"`. 2. **The font file isn’t being loaded at all.** - No `@font-face` rule in your page. - No entry in the style’s `font-faces` property. - The URL in `font-faces` points to a resource that fails CORS or 404s. 3. **The browser simply doesn’t have the font installed** (common on fresh OS installations). In that case the browser’s generic fallback (usually `Arial`, `Helvetica`, or the OS default sans-serif) is used. Because the fallback chain ends with the browser’s generic family, you end up with a “generic” look. --- ## 3. How to make the intended font appear ### Option A – Load the font as a **web font** (the most common approach) 1. **Add a CSS `@font-face` rule** (or use a font-loading library) that declares the exact family name you will use in `text-font`. ```css @font-face { font-family: "MyBrand Font"; src: url("/fonts/MyBrandFont-Regular.woff2") format("woff2"), url("/fonts/MyBrandFont-Regular.woff") format("woff"); font-weight: normal; font-style: normal; } @font-face { font-family: "MyBrand Font"; src: url("/fonts/MyBrandFont-Bold.woff2") format("woff2"), url("/fonts/MyBrandFont-Bold.woff") format("woff"); font-weight: bold; font-style: normal; } ``` 2. **Reference that exact family name** in your style: ```json { "type": "symbol", "layout": { "text-field": ["get", "name"], "text-font": ["MyBrand Font Bold", "Noto Sans Regular"] } } ``` 3. **Make sure the font files are reachable** (CORS headers, correct path, etc.). When the map loads, MapLibre will ask the browser to load the font; once the `document.fonts.ready` promise resolves, the labels will be drawn with your font. ### Option B – Declare the font via the **`font-faces`** style property (works for both GL JS and Native) If you want the same style file to work on MapLibre GL JS **and** MapLibre Native (iOS/Android), use the spec-defined `font-faces` object: ```json { "font-faces": { "MyBrand Font Regular": [ { "url": "https://example.com/fonts/MyBrandFont-Regular.ttf", "unicode-range": ["U+0000-FFFF"] // optional, can limit to the script you need } ], "MyBrand Font Bold": [ { "url": "https://example.com/fonts/MyBrandFont-Bold.ttf" } ] } } ``` *Important notes* * The `url` must be **fetchable by the browser** when you run GL JS (i.e., it must be served over HTTP(S) with proper CORS). * Native platforms read the same `font-faces` entries, but they fetch the files directly from the device or from a network URL, so the same URL works for both environments. ### Option C – Serve **glyph PBFs** (the classic Mapbox-style approach) If you prefer the original “glyph-server” model (or you need the same look on Native **without** relying on local fonts), add a `glyphs` URL to the style and host the appropriate PBFs. ```json { "glyphs": "https://my.cdn.com/fonts/{fontstack}/{range}.pbf" } ``` * Then make sure the folder structure matches the font-stack names (`MyBrand%20Font%20Bold/0-255.pbf`, etc.). * This approach works on **both GL JS and Native** without any fallback logic, but it requires you to generate the PBFs (e.g., with Font Maker or `fontnik`) unless you can reuse an existing set (Noto, OpenMapTiles, etc.). > **When to choose this?** > *You have a brand-specific font that must look identical on every device, including offline Native apps, and you don’t want to rely on the user’s system fonts.* --- ## 4. Quick checklist – “Why isn’t my font showing?” | ✅ Check | What to verify | |---------|----------------| | **Font-face name matches** | The string in `text-font` **exactly** matches the `font-family` declared in CSS or the key in `font-faces`. | | **Font file is reachable** | Open the URL in a browser → returns the font file with `Access-Control-Allow-Origin:*` (or your domain). | | **CORS is correct** | For GL JS, the font file must allow cross-origin requests. | | **Browser has loaded the font** | Open DevTools → `document.fonts.ready` resolves, or look at the **Network** tab for the font request. | | **`font-faces` entry (if used) is correct** | The JSON key matches the `text-font` name, and the `url` points to a valid TTF/OTF/WOFF2 file. | | **No `glyphs` URL** | If you *do* have a `glyphs` field, the engine will still try to fetch glyph PBFs first; missing PBFs will trigger the local-font fallback (still generic if the font isn’t loaded). | | **Local-Ideograph handling** | For CJK characters, `localIdeographFontFamily` overrides `text-font`. If you need a specific CJK font, set `localIdeographFontFamily` to that family; otherwise leave the default. | If all of the above are satisfied and you still see a generic font, open the browser console and look for warnings like: ``` Unable to load glyph range ... Rendering codepoint U+... locally instead. ``` or ``` Failed to load font "MyBrand Font" from URL ... ``` Those messages point directly to the missing resource. --- ## 5. TL;DR – What you should do 1. **Confirm you really want to omit `glyphs`.** *If you need pixel-perfect, cross-platform consistency, add a `glyphs` URL.* 2. **If you stay in “local-fonts mode”:** * Load the font via CSS `@font-face` **or** declare it in the style’s `font-faces`. * Ensure the name you use in `text-font` matches the declared family name exactly. * Verify the font file loads (no CORS errors). 3. **Test:** ```js // Wait for fonts before creating the map (optional but clean) document.fonts.ready.then(() => { const map = new maplibregl.Map({ /* … */ }); }); ``` 4. **If you later need the same style on Native:** * Keep the `font-faces` entries (they work on both SDKs). * Or add a `glyphs` URL and host the PBFs for full offline support. --- ## 6. Gotchas & advanced notes | Topic | Detail | |-------|--------| | **Weight & style keywords** | In local-fonts mode, `text-font` can contain `"Bold"` or `"Italic"` as separate entries (e.g., `["MyBrand Font Bold", "MyBrand Font"]`). The engine will request the appropriate weight from the same family if the font file includes it, otherwise the browser will synthesize it. | | **Multiple fallback fonts** | You can list several families: `["MyBrand Font", "Noto Sans Regular", "Arial Unicode MS Regular"]`. The first one that loads will be used for the whole label (GL JS treats the list as a *single* fallback, not per-character). | | **CJK local rendering** | `localIdeographFontFamily` defaults to `'sans-serif'`. If you want a specific CJK font, set it to that family name (must be installed or declared via `@font-face`). Setting it to `false` forces the engine to request glyph PBFs for CJK – only do this if you have a pre-generated CJK glyph set and you really need those exact shapes. | | **Right-to-left scripts** | Since GL JS 6.9.0 you no longer need `setRTLTextPlugin`. The local-fonts fallback works for Arabic, Hebrew, etc., as long as the font you load supports those scripts. | | **Complex scripts (Devanagari, Thai, Khmer, etc.)** | From GL JS 6.15.0 onward these are rendered via the browser’s shaping engine, *ignoring* glyph PBFs. Therefore the `font-faces` entry (or a system font) is the only way to control their appearance. | | **Native only** | MapLibre Native **does not** support the “omit `glyphs`” fallback. If you plan to run the same style on Native, you must provide a `glyphs` URL (or embed the font via `font-faces` and rely on HarfBuzz shaping). | | **Performance** | Local-fonts mode eliminates the many small network requests that a glyph server would make (especially for CJK). The trade-off is that you depend on the client’s font rendering quality and on the availability of the font files. | --- ### Bottom line - **No `glyphs` → expected local-font behavior.** - The generic font you see simply means the requested font isn’t available locally. - Fix it by **loading the font yourself** (CSS `@font-face` or `font-faces`) and making sure the name matches, **or** by adding a proper `glyphs` URL if you need a guaranteed, server-served look across all platforms. That’s all there is to it—no bug to file, just a configuration choice. Happy labeling!

Description: implicit — offline/local fonts on MapLibre Native, not GL JS
prompt: I'm building an offline map app with MapLibre Native on Android and want labels to render in local device fonts without running a glyphs server. What's the right way to configure this?
[groq-gpt-oss] evals/prompts/lib/skill-p:
Below is a **step-by-step recipe** for an Android MapLibre Native app that works completely offline and draws its labels from the device’s own font files instead of a remote glyph-PBF server.

---

## 1. What the engine actually needs

| Component | What it does | What you must provide for an offline build |
|-----------|--------------|--------------------------------------------|
| **`glyphs` URL** | The engine expects a URL template `…/{fontstack}/{range}.pbf`. If the request fails, GL Native **does not fall back** to a local renderer (unlike GL JS ≥ 5.11). | You still have to set a `glyphs` field, but you can point it at a **local, empty** PBF tree (or a tiny “dummy” set that ships with the app). The engine will try to load it, fail quickly, and then move on to the `font-faces` mapping. |
| **`font-faces`** | Maps each `text-font` name used in the style to one or more font files (TTF/OTF) that the native runtime loads via HarfBuzz. | Put the desired font files in your APK (e.g. `assets/fonts/…`) and list them in `font-faces`. This is the only way to get true **local-font rendering** on Native. |
| **`localIdeographFontFamily`** | Only GL JS has a special “render CJK locally” switch. Native does **not** have an equivalent; CJK must be served as glyph PBFs or you accept the (usually acceptable) fallback to the system’s default CJK font when the glyph request fails. | For most offline apps you can simply let the fallback use the device’s built-in CJK font – no extra work needed. If you need a specific CJK face, bundle a CJK TTF and reference it in `font-faces` (the same as any other script). |

> **Bottom line:**  
> *You cannot completely omit `glyphs`, but you can make it a no-op and let `font-faces` drive the rendering.*  

---

## 2. Prepare the font files

1. **Choose the fonts** you want to use. The safest universal choice is the **Noto** family (Google’s “no tofu” fonts).  
   * `NotoSans-Regular.ttf` – Latin, Greek, Cyrillic, etc.  
   * `NotoSansArabic-Regular.ttf` – Arabic, Hebrew, Syriac, etc.  
   * `NotoSansDevanagari-Regular.ttf` – Devanagari, Bengali, etc.  
   * `NotoSansCJKsc-Regular.otf` – Simplified Chinese (or the appropriate CJK variant).  

2. **Copy them into the Android assets folder** (or `res/raw` if you prefer). Example layout:

```
app/
 └─ src/
     └─ main/
         └─ assets/
             └─ fonts/
                 ├─ NotoSans-Regular.ttf
                 ├─ NotoSansArabic-Regular.ttf
                 ├─ NotoSansDevanagari-Regular.ttf
                 └─ NotoSansCJKsc-Regular.otf
```

3. **(Optional) Sub-set the fonts** if you want to keep the APK small. Tools like [pyftsubset](https://github.com/fonttools/fonttools) let you keep only the Unicode ranges you actually need.

---

## 3. Create a minimal *glyphs* tree (offline-only)

Even though you won’t use the glyph PBFs, the style must contain a valid `glyphs` template. The easiest approach is to ship an **empty folder** that mimics the expected structure:

```
assets/
 └─ glyphs/
     └─ Noto%20Sans/
         └─ 0-255.pbf   (a 0-byte file or a tiny placeholder)
```

*Why a placeholder?*  
MapLibre Native will try to load `…/Noto%20Sans/0-255.pbf`. If the file exists (even empty) the request resolves instantly, avoiding a network error log. If you prefer not to ship any PBF at all, just point `glyphs` at a non-existent local URL (e.g. `file:///android_asset/glyphs/{fontstack}/{range}.pbf`); the engine will get a “file not found” error and then fall back to `font-faces`.

**Example `glyphs` entry in the style:**

```json
"glyphs": "file:///android_asset/glyphs/{fontstack}/{range}.pbf"
```

---

## 4. Add a `font-faces` block to the style

The `font-faces` property lives at the **root** of the style JSON (same level as `sources`, `layers`, etc.). It maps the exact strings you will use in `text-font` to the font files you bundled.

```json
{
  "version": 8,
  "glyphs": "file:///android_asset/glyphs/{fontstack}/{range}.pbf",
  "font-faces": {
    "Noto Sans Regular": [
      {
        "url": "file:///android_asset/fonts/NotoSans-Regular.ttf",
        "unicode-range": ["U+0000-00FF", "U+0100-024F"]   // Latin, Latin-1-Supplement, etc.
      }
    ],
    "Noto Sans Arabic": [
      {
        "url": "file:///android_asset/fonts/NotoSansArabic-Regular.ttf",
        "unicode-range": ["U+0600-06FF", "U+0750-077F", "U+08A0-08FF"]
      }
    ],
    "Noto Sans Devanagari": [
      {
        "url": "file:///android_asset/fonts/NotoSansDevanagari-Regular.ttf",
        "unicode-range": ["U+0900-097F"]
      }
    ],
    "Noto Sans CJK SC": [
      {
        "url": "file:///android_asset/fonts/NotoSansCJKsc-Regular.otf",
        "unicode-range": ["U+4E00-9FFF", "U+3400-4DBF"]
      }
    ]
  },
  "layers": [
    {
      "id": "place-labels",
      "type": "symbol",
      "source": "osm",
      "source-layer": "place",
      "layout": {
        "text-field": ["get", "name"],
        "text-font": [
          "Noto Sans CJK SC",
          "Noto Sans Arabic",
          "Noto Sans Devanagari",
          "Noto Sans Regular"
        ],
        "text-size": 12
      },
      "paint": {
        "text-color": "#222"
      }
    }
  ]
}
```

### Key points

* **Exact name match** – The string in `text-font` **must** be identical to the key in `font-faces`.  
* **Unicode-range** – Optional but recommended; it tells the engine which characters to pull from which file. If omitted, the engine will try the first matching file for every code-point.  
* **Order matters** – `text-font` is a fallback list. The first entry that contains the needed glyph (via `unicode-range`) wins.  

---

## 5. Load the style in Android

```kotlin
import org.maplibre.android.maps.MapView
import org.maplibre.android.maps.Style
import org.maplibre.android.maps.MapLibre

class OfflineMapActivity : AppCompatActivity() {

    private lateinit var mapView: MapView

    override fun onCreate(savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
        super.onCreate(savedInstanceState)

        // Initialise the SDK (required once per process)
        MapLibre.getInstance(this)

        mapView = MapView(this)
        setContentView(mapView)

        // Point the style to the bundled JSON file (also in assets)
        mapView.getMapAsync { mapboxMap ->
            mapboxMap.setStyle(
                Style.Builder()
                    .fromUri("asset://offline-style.json")   // <-- your style from step 4
            ) { style ->
                // style is ready – you can now add sources, layers, etc.
            }
        }
    }

    // Remember to forward lifecycle events to the MapView …
}
```

*The `asset://` scheme tells the native SDK to read the file from `src/main/assets/`.*  

If you prefer to keep the style in code (e.g. generated at runtime), you can call `Style.Builder().fromJson(styleJsonString)` instead.

---

## 6. (Optional) Bundle a tiny glyph-PBF set for Latin

If you want to avoid the “file not found” log for the Latin range, you can generate a **single** PBF that contains the most common Latin glyphs (0-255). The easiest way is to copy the pre-built file from the public MapLibre demo:

```
https://demotiles.maplibre.org/font/Noto%20Sans/0-255.pbf
```

Place it under `assets/glyphs/Noto%20Sans/0-255.pbf`. The engine will load it instantly, and the rest of the ranges (which you never request because the local font covers them) will still fall back to `font-faces`.

---

## 7. Handling CJK, Arabic, and complex scripts

| Script | How it is rendered on Native (offline) | What you must do |
|--------|----------------------------------------|------------------|
| **CJK (Chinese, Japanese, Korean)** | If the glyph request fails, the engine falls back to the **system CJK font** (the device’s built-in font). | No extra work. If you want a specific CJK face, add it to `font-faces` as shown above. |
| **Arabic / Hebrew (right-to-left)** | HarfBuzz shaping is built-in (since Native v11.13). The engine will use the `font-faces` entry that matches the script. | Ensure the appropriate Noto-Arabic (or any RTL) font is listed in `font-faces`. No `setRTLTextPlugin` needed. |
| **Devanagari, Thai, Khmer, Myanmar, etc.** | These scripts require **grapheme-cluster shaping**. Native does this via HarfBuzz, **ignoring the glyph PBFs**. | Provide the script-specific TTF/OTF in `font-faces` (as in the example). The `unicode-range` entry guarantees the right file is chosen. |
| **Latin / Cyrillic / Greek** | If you ship a tiny PBF (step 6) the engine will use it; otherwise it will fall back to the local TTF you listed. | Either keep the tiny PBF or rely solely on the TTF. Both work offline. |

---

## 8. Common pitfalls & troubleshooting

| Symptom | Likely cause | Fix |
|---------|--------------|-----|
| **Labels disappear completely** | `text-font` name does not match any key in `font-faces`. | Verify spelling, spaces, and case. Use the exact string from the style. |
| **Wrong font appears (e.g., Latin text shows a system sans-serif instead of Noto)** | The `unicode-range` of the listed font does not include the code-points you are rendering. | Expand the `unicode-range` or add another entry that covers the missing block. |
| **CJK characters look blocky or missing** | The device’s default CJK font is missing (rare on Android) **or** you set `localIdeographFontFamily` in GL JS but not in Native. | Add a CJK TTF to `font-faces` (e.g., `NotoSansCJKsc-Regular.otf`). |
| **Console shows “Unable to load glyph range …” repeatedly** | The placeholder glyph tree is missing or the `file:///android_asset/...` URL is wrong. | Double-check the path, ensure the file exists in `assets/glyphs/...`, and that the URL uses `file:///android_asset/`. |
| **Arabic text is displayed left-to-right** | You are using a pre-v6.9.0 MapLibre GL JS style (unlikely on Native) or the font you supplied lacks Arabic glyphs. | Use a proper Arabic font (NotoSansArabic) and ensure the `unicode-range` covers U+0600-06FF. |
| **App crashes on map load** | `MapLibre.getInstance(this)` not called before creating the `MapView`. | Call `MapLibre.getInstance(context)` early (e.g., in `Application.onCreate`). |

---

Description: explicit — right-to-left Arabic and Hebrew labels on GL JS 6
prompt: My MapLibre GL JS 6 map has Arabic and Hebrew place names. What do I need to set up so those labels read right-to-left with the Arabic letters joined correctly?
[groq-gpt-oss] evals/prompts/lib/skill-p:
## TL;DR * **Use MapLibre GL JS ≥ 6.9.0** – the engine now shapes Arabic/Hebrew itself, so you **don’t need the old `setRTLTextPlugin`**. * Add a **proper Arabic/Hebrew font** (e.g. *Noto Sans Arabic* / *Noto Sans Hebrew*) to the style’s `font-faces` (or serve its glyph PBFs). * Make sure every layer that draws place-names lists that font in its `text-font` fallback array. * If you are on an older version (< 6.9.0) you must load the RTL-text plugin **once, before creating the map**. Below is a complete checklist, code snippets and a short troubleshooting table. --- ## 1. Verify the MapLibre version ```bash npm list maplibre-gl # or check package.json ``` * **≥ 6.9.0** – native shaping, no plugin required. * **< 6.9.0** – you must load the RTL plugin (see § 4). > **Why it matters** – Before 6.9.0 the core renderer only knew left-to-right scripts. The plugin supplies a HarfBuzz-based shaper that joins Arabic letters and reverses the order for Hebrew. From 6.9.0 onward the shaper is built-in, making the workflow simpler and the map offline-friendly. --- ## 2. Provide a font that contains the Arabic/Hebrew glyphs ### 2.1. Preferred approach – **`font-faces`** (works for both GL JS and Native) Add a `font-faces` entry to the root of your style JSON. The `url` must be reachable by the browser (CORS-enabled if on a different origin). ```json { "version": 8, "glyphs": "https://example.com/fonts/{fontstack}/{range}.pbf", // can stay, not used for Arabic/Hebrew after 6.15.0 "font-faces": { "Noto Sans Arabic": [ { "url": "https://example.com/fonts/NotoSansArabic-Regular.ttf", "unicode-range": ["U+0600-06FF", "U+0750-077F", "U+08A0-08FF", "U+FB50-FDFF", "U+FE70-FEFF", "U+1EE00-1EEFF"] } ], "Noto Sans Hebrew": [ { "url": "https://example.com/fonts/NotoSansHebrew-Regular.ttf", "unicode-range": ["U+0590-05FF", "U+FB1D-FB4F"] } ] }, "layers": [ … ] } ``` * **Unicode-range** is optional but helps the engine skip the file for unrelated code points. * The `url` can point at a local file served via a static-file server, a CDN, or a data-URI (`"url":"data:font/ttf;base64,..."`). ### 2.2. Alternative – serve **glyph-PBFs** (only needed for pre-6.15.0) If you prefer the classic glyph-server route, copy the pre-built PBF tree for *Noto Sans Arabic* and *Noto Sans Hebrew* from the OpenMapTiles `fonts` repo and host it under the same `glyphs` URL template. > **Note:** Since GL JS 6.15.0 the engine will ignore those PBFs for complex scripts (Arabic, Hebrew, Devanagari, etc.) and will always use the `font-faces` files, but keeping the PBFs does no harm and helps older native builds. --- ## 3. Reference the font in your style layers Every symbol layer that shows place names should list the Arabic/Hebrew font **first** (or at least before a generic fallback). Example: ```json { "id": "place-labels", "type": "symbol", "source": "osm", "source-layer": "place", "layout": { "text-field": ["get", "name"], "text-font": ["Noto Sans Arabic", "Noto Sans Hebrew", "Noto Sans Regular"], // fallback order "text-size": 12, "text-anchor": "center" }, "paint": { "text-color": "#222" } } ``` * The engine automatically detects the script of each label (by Unicode code points) and picks the first font that covers those characters. * If a label contains mixed scripts (e.g., Arabic + Latin), the first font that can render the whole grapheme cluster is used; otherwise the engine falls back to the next entry. --- ## 4. (Only for GL JS < 6.9.0) Load the RTL-text plugin ```javascript import { setRTLTextPlugin } from 'maplibre-gl'; // Load the plugin *once*, before any map instance is created. setRTLTextPlugin( 'https://unpkg.com/@mapbox/mapbox-gl-rtl-text@0.3.0/dist/mapbox-gl-rtl-text.js', /* lazy */ false // true would load on-demand, but false is recommended for deterministic startup ); ``` * After the plugin is registered, create the map as usual. * The plugin is **not needed** (and will be ignored) on versions ≥ 6.9.0. --- ## 5. Optional: Tweak `localIdeographFontFamily` CJK characters are rendered locally via TinySDF; this setting does **not** affect Arabic/Hebrew. You can leave it at the default: ```javascript const map = new maplibregl.Map({ container: 'map', style: 'https://example.com/style.json', // No need to touch localIdeographFontFamily for RTL scripts }); ``` --- ## 6. Description: implicit — Devanagari labels drawn letter by letter
prompt: Hindi labels on my MapLibre GL JS map come out wrong: vowel signs and conjuncts land in the wrong place, as if each letter were drawn on its own. My style has a glyphs URL that serves Noto Sans Devanagari. How do I fix it?
[groq-gpt-oss] evals/prompts/lib/skill-p:
### Why Devanagari looks “letter-by-letter”

Devanagari (and other Indic scripts) needs **grapheme-cluster shaping** – a consonant + vowel sign, a conjunct, etc. A glyph-PBF contains only *single* code-points, so when the style points at a `glyphs` URL the engine can only draw each code-point separately.  
Since **MapLibre GL JS 6.15.0** the renderer falls back to the browser’s text engine for those scripts, but **only if the style tells the engine to use a local font** (via `font-faces`). If the style only has a `glyphs` URL, the old “draw each code-point” path is still used and you get the misplaced vowel signs you’re seeing.

### Fix – let the browser do the shaping

1. **Upgrade to a recent GL JS version**  
   ```text
   >= 6.15.0   (6.9.0 already supports RTL, 6.7.0 added basic shaping, 6.15.0 makes it the default for Indic scripts)
   ```
   Anything older will still draw Devanagari from the glyph PBFs.

2. **Add a `font-faces` entry for the Devanagari font**  
   The `font-faces` property maps the `text-font` name you use in the style to a real TTF/OTF that the browser can load.

   ```json
   {
     "version": 8,
     "glyphs": "https://my-tileserver.example.com/fonts/{fontstack}/{range}.pbf",
     "font-faces": {
       "Noto Sans Devanagari Regular": [
         {
           "url": "https://my-tileserver.example.com/webfonts/NotoSansDevanagari-Regular.ttf",
           "unicode-range": ["U+0900-097F"]
         }
       ]
     },
     "layers": [
       {
         "id": "place-labels-hi",
         "type": "symbol",
         "source": "osm",
         "source-layer": "place",
         "layout": {
           "text-field": ["get", "name:hi"],
           "text-font": ["Noto Sans Devanagari Regular", "Noto Sans Regular"],   // fallback order
           "text-size": 12
         }
       }
     ]
   }
   ```

   * **`url` must be reachable by the browser** (CORS-enabled, same-origin or with proper `Access-Control-Allow-Origin`).  
   * The `unicode-range` limits the file to Devanagari code-points; you can omit it if the file only contains that script.

3. **(Optional) Remove the Devanagari range from the `glyphs` tree**  
   The glyph server will still be queried for any Devanagari range that isn’t covered by a `font-faces` entry, but the browser-shaped font will win. To avoid unnecessary network traffic you can simply not serve Devanagari PBFs, or delete the `Noto Sans Devanagari` folder from the glyph tree.

4. **Make sure the `text-font` list in every layer that shows Hindi includes the Devanagari entry**  
   ```json
   "text-font": ["Noto Sans Devanagari Regular", "Noto Sans Regular"]
   ```
   The first name that matches a `font-faces` entry is used; the second is a fallback for any characters outside the Devanagari range.

5. **Test in the browser console**  
   ```js
   map.getStyle().fontFaces
   // should show the entry you added
   ```
   If the font fails to load you’ll see a CORS or 404 error in the network tab; fix the URL and retry.

### What if you can’t change the style (e.g. a third-party style)?

* **Inject the `font-faces` at runtime** – after the map is created:

  ```js
  map.setFontFaces({
    "Noto Sans Devanagari Regular": [
      {
        url: "https://my-tileserver.example.com/webfonts/NotoSansDevanagari-Regular.ttf",
        "unicode-range": ["U+0900-097F"]
      }
    ]
  });
  ```

  This works with GL JS ≥ 6.7.0 and does not require editing the JSON style file.

### Quick checklist

| ✅ | Action |
|---|--------|
| **Version** | Use MapLibre GL JS ≥ 6.15.0 (or at least 6.7.0, but 6.15+ is safest). |
| **font-faces** | Add a `font-faces` entry that points to a Devanagari TTF/OTF and limits it to `U+0900-097F`. |
| **text-font** | Include the same name as the first entry in `text-font` arrays for Hindi layers. |
| **CORS** | Ensure the font file is served with `Access-Control-Allow-Origin:*` (or your domain). |
| **Glyphs** | Keep the `glyphs` URL for other scripts; you can omit Devanagari PBFs. |
| **Test** | Verify the network tab shows the TTF being fetched and that Hindi labels render correctly (vowel signs attached, conjuncts formed). |

### TL;DR

1. Upgrade to GL JS ≥ 6.15.0.  
2. Add a `font-faces` entry for **Noto Sans Devanagari** (or any Devanagari TTF you prefer).  
3. Reference that name first in `text-font`.  
4. Ensure the font file is reachable (CORS).  

After those steps the browser’s shaping engine will draw Hindi text correctly, and the glyph-PBF server will no longer be used for Devanagari.
